lesson.title: Turning Slope into Voltage: The Op-Amp Differentiator
lesson.summary: Swapping the input resistor and feedback capacitor of an integrator produces a differentiator, a circuit whose output is proportional to how fast the input is changing rather than to the input's level.
lesson.body:
The differentiator is the integrator's structural mirror image: put the capacitor at the input and keep a resistor as the feedback element.

Current through a capacitor is i = C times dV/dt, the rate form of Q = CV from the capacitor concept, so the current flowing into the virtual-ground node through the input capacitor is C times the rate of change of Vin. That entire current has to flow through the feedback resistor R, since none of it can enter the op-amp's input, producing a voltage across R and hence an output proportional to that current: Vout = -RC times (dVin/dt). Where the integrator accumulates a signal's entire history, the differentiator reports only its instantaneous slope, and throws away the input's actual level entirely.

Take the same R = 10 kilohm, C = 1 microfarad, so RC = 0.01 second. Suppose Vin ramps linearly from 0V to 1V over 2 milliseconds (0.002s), a constant slope of dVin/dt = 1V / 0.002s = 500V per second. Then Vout = -RC times 500V/s = -0.01 times 500 = -5V, held steady for as long as the input keeps rising at that same rate.

This behavior has an important consequence for fast edges. A square wave has, in the idealized limit, an instantaneous jump at each transition, meaning dVin/dt spikes toward infinity for an instant, producing narrow output spikes at every edge rather than a clean copy of the square wave. Real circuits tame this by adding a small resistor in series with the input capacitor to limit the gain at very high frequencies. That same sensitivity to fast changes is the differentiator's chief practical drawback: it amplifies high-frequency noise more strongly than it amplifies the desired signal, since noise typically has large, fast swings, exactly the opposite of the integrator, which tends to smooth high-frequency content out rather than emphasize it.
